'''''Chamaecyparis thyoides''''' ('''Atlantic white cedar''', '''Atlantic white cypress''', '''southern white cedar''', '''whitecedar''', or '''false-cypress''') is a species of conifer in the cypress family, [[Cupressaceae]]. It is native to the Atlantic coast of North America and is found from southern [[Maine]] to [[Georgia (U.S. state)|Georgia]] and along the [[Gulf of Mexico]] coast from [[Florida]] to [[Mississippi]].  It is one of two species of ''[[Chamaecyparis]]'' found in North America.  ''C. thyoides'' resides on the [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]] and [[chamaecyparis lawsoniana|''C. lawsoniana'']] can be found on the [[West Coast of the United States|West Coast]]. There are two geographically isolated [[subspecies]], treated by some botanists as distinct species, by others at just [[variety (biology)|varietal]] rank: ''Chamaecyparis thyoides thyoides'' and ''Chamaecyparis thyoides henryae'' (H.L.Li) E.Murray (syn. ''Chamaecyparis thyoides'' subsp. ''henryae'' (H.L.Li) Little; ''Chamaecyparis henryae'' H.L.Li)<ref name=farjon/><ref name=rushforthc/><ref name="allozyme">{{cite journal|author=Mylecraine KA|title=Geographic allozyme variation in Atlantic white-cedar, Chamaecyparis thyoides (Cupresseceae)|journal=Canadian Journal of Forest Research|date=2004|volume=34|issue=12|pages=2443–2454|doi=10.1139/X04-125|display-authors=etal}}</ref> The species grows in forested [[wetlands]] where they tend to dominate the [[Canopy (biology)|canopy]].  The trees are associated with a wide variety of other wetland species because of their wide north-south range. The remaining populations are now found mostly in remote locations that would be difficult to harvest, so its popularity as a source of [[lumber]] has decreased.

==Distribution and habitat==
''Chamaecyparis thyoides'' grows within 100 miles of the coastline and less than 50 m above sea level<ref name="plantsprofile" /> along much of the [[East Coast of the United States|East Coast]] and [[Gulf Coast of the United States|Gulf Coast]].<ref name=grin>{{GRIN | access-date = 12 December 2017}}</ref>  Rare populations grow in the foothills of the [[Appalachian Mountains]], where the tree may be found up to 460 m above sea level.<ref name=farjon>Farjon, A. (2005). ''Monograph of Cupressaceae and Sciadopitys''. Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew. {{ISBN|1-84246-068-4}}</ref>  Nationally, Atlantic white cedar is protected in the [[Great Dismal Swamp National Wildlife Refuge]], [[Alligator River National Wildlife Refuge]], [[Pinelands National Reserve]], [[Cape Cod National Seashore]], [[Croatan National Forest]], [[Francis Marion National Forest]], [[Ocala National Forest]], and [[Apalachicola National Forest]]. Altered [[fire regime]]s, logging, and draining of wetlands outside of the few protected areas have all contributed to the general decrease in the size and occurrences of Atlantic white cedar stands. The tree is listed as [[Rare species|Rare]] in Georgia and [[New York (state)|New York]], of Special Concern in Maine, and [[Local extinction|Extirpated]] in [[Pennsylvania]].<ref name="plantsprofile" /><ref name="mylecraine_rangewide">{{cite journal|author=Mylecraine KA|title=Rangewide provenance variation in Atlantic white-cedar (Chamaecyparis thyoides): Early survival and growth in New Jersey and North Carolina plantations|journal=Forest Ecology and Management|date=2009|volume=216|issue=1|pages=91–104|doi=10.1016/j.foreco.2005.05.053|display-authors=etal}}</ref><ref name="biological_report">{{cite journal|last1=Laderman|first1=AD|title=The ecology of the Atlantic white cedar wetlands: a community profile|journal=US Fish and Wildlife Service Biological Report|date=1989|volume=85|issue=7.21|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=y0i3tekDNDAC}}</ref> In Mississippi, the species is at risk of extirpation as a consequence of [[overexploitation]], changes in land use, and extreme weather events.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hale |first1=Clayton W |last2=Granger |first2=Joshua J |last3=Correa |first3=Sandra B |last4=DuBien |first4=Janice L |last5=Siegert |first5=Courtney M |date=2022-05-07 |title=Atlantic White-Cedar (''Chamaecyparis thyoides'' [L.] B.S.P.) Response Post-Hurricane Disturbance |journal=Forest Science |volume=68 |issue=3 |pages=270–282 |doi=10.1093/forsci/fxac007 |issn=0015-749X|doi-access=free }}</ref>

''Chamaecyparis thyoides'' lives almost exclusively in freshwater wetlands and is considered an [[Wetland indicator status|obligate wetland species]]. It prefers habitats where the soil is saturated with water at least during the majority of the growing season. The soils in these regions have a thick organic layer, often classified as a [[soil horizon#Diagnostic surface horizons of mineral soils|histic surface horizon]], with sandy material at greater depths and poor drainage. Atlantic white cedar wetlands are acidic and there is little oxygen stored in the soil because water has displaced the air. Plants that live in these environments must be specially adapted to such conditions.

===Ecology===
[[Red maple]] and [[Nyssa sylvatica|black gum]] trees are often found in the canopy along with Atlantic white cedar throughout its range. [[Sphagnum]] mosses also often grow in these wetlands.<ref name="mylecraine_rangewide" /><ref name="biological_report" />  The caterpillar of the [[Hessel's hairstreak]] butterfly feeds exclusively on ''C. thyoides,'' where its green color helps to [[camouflage]] it.<ref name="bright_butterflies">{{cite journal|last1=Bright|first1=S|last2=Charny|first2=V|last3=Howell|first3=WM|title=Butterflies: new records for Alabama|journal=Journal of the Alabama Academy of Science|date=2013|volume=84|issue=1|page=37}}</ref>

The trees themselves grow on [[hummocks]], small mounds, with water pooling in the depressions surrounding them.  This keeps the tree from being underwater year-round and helps to protect from floods. The tree benefits from periodic low-intensity fires which expose [[seedlings]] to sunlight and limit competition with other canopy [[flora]], particularly red maple. Too frequent or intense fires or flooding can damage seedlings stored in the top layer of soil and full-grown trees.<ref name="plantsprofile" />

==Description==
''Chamaecyparis thyoides'' is a [[Pinophyta|coniferous]] [[tree]] usually growing to {{convert|20|–|28|m|abbr=on}} (but may grow up to {{convert|35|m|abbr=on}}) tall with an average diameter of {{convert|0.8|m|abbr=on}}, up to {{convert|2|m|abbr=on}}, and feathery foliage in moderately flattened sprays, green to [[glaucous]] blue-green in color. The [[leaf|leaves]] are scale-like, {{convert|2|–|4|mm|frac=32|abbr=on}} long, and produced in opposite [[decussate]] pairs on somewhat flattened shoots; seedlings up to a year old have needle-like leaves. The tree is bare of branches for three-fourths of the [[trunk (botany)|trunk]] height and the [[bark (botany)|bark]] can be ash-gray to reddish brown.  Bark is smooth on juveniles, but mature trees have deep ridges and bark as thick as {{convert|5|cm|frac=4|abbr=on}}. ''C. thyoides'' is [[monoecious]], so a single tree will carry both the pollen and seeds needed for reproduction in cones.  The [[conifer cone|seed cones]] are [[globose]], {{convert|4|–|9|mm|frac=32|abbr=on}} diameter, with 6-10 scales (1-2 seeds per scale), green or purple, maturing to brown in 5–7 months after pollination. The pollen cones are yellow but turn brown as the tree matures, {{convert|1.5|–|3|mm|frac=32|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1|–|2|mm|frac=32|abbr=on}} broad, releasing their yellow pollen once a year in spring.<ref name=farjon/><ref name=rushforthc>Rushforth, K. (1987). ''Conifers''. Helm {{ISBN|0-7470-2801-X}}.</ref><ref name="mylecraine_rangewide"/><ref name="biological_report"/>  The tree begins bearing seeds at 4–5 years, but does not reach full maturity and start producing cones until it is 10-20 years old. Seeds are dispersed nearly every year and travel by wind.<ref name="dendrology">{{cite book|last1=Harlow|first1=William Morehouse|title=Textbook of Dendrology|date=1979|publisher=McGraw-Hill, Inc.|isbn=0-07-026570-4|pages=200–201}}</ref>  Height and diameter of the tree increase steadily until the tree is 50 years old, at which point height growth slows.  Both height and diameter no longer increase once the tree is 100 years old.  Stands are generally all younger than 200 years, though some trees as old as 1000 years have been reported. Because they have relatively shallow roots, ''C. thyoides'' are vulnerable to being blown over by wind.<ref name="plantsprofile">{{cite web|title=Plants Profile for Chamaecyparis thyoides|url=http://plants.usda.gov/plant-profile?symbol=chth2|website=USDA Natural Resource Conservation Service}}</ref><ref name="crawford">{{cite journal |author=Crawford ER |display-authors=etal |date=2007 |title=Influence of environment and substrate quality on root decomposition in naturally regenerating and restored Atlantic white cedar wetlands |journal=Wetlands |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=1–11 |doi=10.1672/0277-5212(2007)27[1:ioeasq]2.0.co;2|s2cid=12678061 }}</ref>

===Subspecies variation===
*''Chamaecyparis thyoides thyoides'': Leaves and immature cones usually glaucous blue-green; cones mature to dark brown-black; facial leaves flat, not ridged, but with visible [[Gland (botany)|glands]]. 
*''Chamaecyparis thyoides henryae'': Leaves and immature cones green, not glaucous; cones mature to light brown; facial leaves with a longitudinal ridge with glands less obvious or absent.<ref name="farjon" /><ref name="plantsprofile" /><ref name="biological_report" />

==Cultivation and uses==
[[File:Atlantic White Cypress Chatsworth NJ 1.jpg|thumb|right|upright=1.13|Foliage and seed cones]]
''Chamaecyparis thyoides'' is of some importance in [[horticulture]], with several [[cultivar]]s of varying crown shape, growth rates and foliage color having been selected for garden planting. Named cultivars include 'Aurea' (yellow foliage), 'Heatherbun' (dwarf, purple in winter),<ref name="cope_cultivars">{{cite book|last1=Cope|first1=EA; illustrated by Bent King|title=Native and Cultivated Conifers of Northeastern North America: a guide|date=1986|publisher=Cornell University Press|location=Ithaca, N.Y.|isbn=0-8014-1721-X|page=68}}</ref> 'Andelyensis' (dwarf, dense foliage), 'Ericoides' (juvenile foliage), and 'Glauca' (strongly glaucous foliage).<ref name=rushforthc/>  In some locations, particularly [[Mobile County, Alabama]], the tree is cultivated as a [[Christmas tree]].<ref name="ward_commercial" />

===Wood===
Its wood is considered hardy, as it is resistant to decay and warping in a variety of temperatures and moisture levels.  The most common use of white cedar wood is lumber, for which stands usually require 70 years of growth from [[germination]] to harvest.  The lumber may be used in house construction, though scarcity of Atlantic white cedar makes it difficult to use as the primary material.  The wood was favored for roof shingles because it is lightweight, but has since been replaced by cheaper and more fire-resistant materials such as asphalt.  The durability of the [[heartwood]] makes it popular for use as siding and paneling, and the less resistant sapwood has been used for interior finishes. White cedar lumber has also been used in [[Boat building|boat construction]], but this requires much older, larger trees. [[North Carolina]] is the greatest producer of lumber for boat construction because it has the greatest number of [[Old-growth forest|old-growth]] ''C. thyoides'' forests.  Other uses include fencing, telephone and electric poles, woodenware, [[Duck decoy (model)|duck decoys]], lawn furniture, and as Christmas trees.<ref name="ward_commercial">{{cite journal|last1=Ward|first1=Daniel|title=Commercial Utilization of Atlantic white cedar (Chamaecyparis thyoides, Cuppressaceae)|journal=Economic Botany|date=1989|volume=43|issue=3|pages=386–415|jstor=4255181|doi=10.1007/bf02858736|s2cid=3200627}}</ref><ref>Peattie, Donald Culross.  Trees You Want to Know.  Whitman Publishing Company, Racine, Wisconsin, 1934 p31</ref>

== Conservation ==
Prior to [[European colonization of the Americas]], there were an estimated {{Convert|500,000|acre|ha}} of swamps and bogs dominated by stands of Atlantic white cedars. At present, less than {{Convert|100,000|acre|ha}} still remain.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jetton |first1=Robert |last2=Whittier |first2=W. Andrew |date=2019 |title=Effect of Seed Coat Sterilization and Photoperiod Treatments on the Germination of Atlantic White-Cedar Seeds |url=https://camcore.cnr.ncsu.edu/files/2020/04/Effect-of-Seed-Coat-Sterilization-and-Photoperiod-Treatments-on-the-Germination-on-Atlantic-White-Cedar-Seeds-2.pdf |journal=Tree Planters' Notes |volume=62}}</ref> Though the tree is not listed as threatened, Atlantic white cedar wetlands are considered a globally threatened ecosystem, and often serve as [[carbon sinks]] because of their [[peat]]-building abilities.<ref name="mylecraine_rangewide" /><ref name="biological_report" /><ref name="crawford" /> Since 2012, ''ex situ'' gene conservation efforts of Atlantic white cedars have been ongoing at [[North Carolina State University]] and the [[United States Forest Service]].
